subject: Business
title: Bitcoin: Money Without Banks
description: A short lesson to help you apply Bitcoin: Money Without Banks.

hook.text: In 2008, someone named Satoshi Nakamoto published a nine-page paper. It proposed money without any central authority.

buildup.text: Bitcoin uses a decentralized ledger — the blockchain — where every transaction is verified by a network, not a bank.

discovery.text: No government can print more Bitcoin. Supply is capped at 21 million coins, enforced by code, not policy.

twist.text: Bitcoin's price swings wildly — 80% drops are common. That volatility undermines its use as everyday money.

climax.text: Whether Bitcoin is digital gold, a currency, or a speculative bubble is still debated by economists worldwide.

punchline.text: Bitcoin proved money can exist without banks.

quiz.question: What limits Bitcoin's supply?
options: Code that caps the total at 21 million coins
A committee of miners that votes on supply
The cost of electricity to mine new coins

details.summary: Bitcoin, launched in 2009 by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto, is a decentralized digital currency that operates without banks or governments. It uses blockchain technology and cryptographic proof to enable peer-to-peer transactions verified by a global network of computers.
details.whyItMatters: Bitcoin challenged the assumption that money requires trusted intermediaries. Whether it becomes mainstream currency or remains a speculative asset, it sparked a revolution in thinking about what money can be in the digital age.
takeaways: Bitcoin operates without central banks or government control
Blockchain technology creates a transparent, tamper-resistant transaction ledger
A fixed supply cap of 21 million bitcoins makes it inherently deflationary

faq.question: How does Bitcoin work without a central authority?
faq.answer: Miners compete to validate transactions using computational power. Valid transactions are grouped into blocks added to a permanent chain. The consensus mechanism ensures all participants agree on the ledger state without needing a central authority to arbitrate.

faq.question: Why is Bitcoin's supply limited to 21 million coins?
faq.answer: The protocol's code enforces a hard cap to create digital scarcity, mimicking gold's finite supply. Mining rewards halve roughly every four years. This fixed supply contrasts with fiat currencies that central banks can print, making Bitcoin deflationary by design.
